title: The Devoted Friend
text:
Little Hans was an honest fellow who grew the loveliest garden in the countryside. His dearest friend, as he believed, was the rich Miller. The Miller loved to say that real friends should have everything in common, and he never passed Hans's garden without filling a big basket with flowers or plums. He never gave anything in return.

In winter, when Hans had no flowers to sell and went hungry, the Miller did not visit. People in trouble should be left alone, he explained to his family, and anyway it might make Hans envious to see their warm kitchen. In spring he promised to give Hans his old broken wheelbarrow. From then on, he reminded Hans of this generosity every time he wanted something. Hans gave him a plank, carried his sack of flour to market, mended his barn roof and drove his sheep to the mountain, while his own garden went to weeds.

One stormy night the Miller knocked at Hans's door. His son had fallen from a ladder, and someone must fetch the doctor. He would not lend his new lantern in case it was lost. Hans went out into the dark and rain, found the doctor, and on the way home lost his path on the moor and drowned in a deep pool.

At the funeral the Miller walked at the head of the procession as Hans's best friend. Afterward he remarked that Hans's death was a great loss to him, because he had as good as given him his wheelbarrow and now did not know what to do with it.
lesson: Judge a friendship by what is done, not by what is said about it. If one side always takes, it is not friendship, so do not be that side.
source: Oscar Wilde, The Devoted Friend, in The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1888)
